sections.title: A famine in a year with more rice
sections.intro_md:
In 1943 between about **800,000 and 3.8 million** people died of hunger in Bengal; the scholarly consensus is about **2.1 million**. The natural explanation is that there was not enough food. That explanation is mostly wrong. Rice supply in 1943 was only about 5% below the average of the previous five years, and about 13% **higher** than in 1941, a year with no famine.

A boy growing up in Santiniketan, Amartya Sen, saw the dying. Decades later he turned the puzzle into economics. People starve, he argued, not only when food is scarce but when their *claim* on food collapses: wages stall, prices soar, and the labourer who sold his work for rice can no longer buy it.

That is today's subject in miniature. Economics studies **scarcity**: the fact that wants outrun the means to meet them. But scarcity is never just a number of sacks in a warehouse. It is about who can command what, at what price, and what each person gives up to get it.

spotlights.name: The Bengal famine of 1943
spotlights.spot_it: Black and white newspaper photographs of skeletal people on Calcutta pavements, printed by The Statesman in August 1943.
spotlights.story_md: Wartime Bengal had lost rice imports from Burma, suffered a cyclone in 1942, and was flooded with military spending. Prices of rice shot up far faster than the wages of fishermen, barbers, craftsmen and landless labourers. The colonial government denied there was a famine for months. The Calcutta paper **The Statesman** broke the silence by printing photographs of the dead in August 1943, defying censorship. The Famine Inquiry Commission of 1945 judged the harvest shortfall at roughly three weeks of supply: serious, not fatal by itself. Others argue harvest losses were far larger, closer to a quarter. The debate is still live, and that is part of the lesson.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the clearest modern case that hunger is about access to food, not only its amount.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bengal 1943: the granaries were not empty, the pockets were.

spotlights.name: Amartya Sen's entitlement idea
spotlights.spot_it: A grey-haired economist from Santiniketan, named by Rabindranath Tagore, who asks who can buy the food, not how much food exists.
spotlights.story_md: Sen was born in **Santiniketan** in 1933; Tagore chose his name. In *Poverty and Famines* (1981) he described each person's **entitlement**: the bundle of goods they can command through what they own, grow, earn or receive. In Bengal an urban war boom pushed food prices up, so rural workers' entitlements collapsed even though the rice was there. In 1999 he wrote that no famine has ever taken place in a functioning democracy, because a free press and voters make hunger politically fatal. Sen won the 1998 Nobel prize in economics and the Bharat Ratna in 1999.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It moved economics from counting goods to asking who has a claim on them.
spotlights.memory_hook: Not how much rice, but whose rice.

compare.difference: Malthus saw famine as too many mouths for too little food; Sen showed it can strike when food is plentiful but claims on it collapse.

sections.title: What economics actually studies
sections.intro_md:
Most people think economics is about money, the stock market or GDP. Those are its objects, not its subject. The definition most textbooks still quote comes from **Lionel Robbins** in 1932: economics is the science which studies human behaviour as a relationship between **ends and scarce means** which have alternative uses.

Unpack that and you get three conditions. You want several things (ends). Your means to get them, such as time, money, land, attention or labour, are limited (scarce). And those means can be used in more than one way (alternative uses). When all three hold, you must choose, and every choice has a cost: the next best thing you did not do. A billionaire with one evening faces scarcity. So does a farmer with one acre, a government with one budget and a country with one river.

Economics then splits in two. **Microeconomics** studies choices by people, firms and markets. **Macroeconomics** studies the whole economy: output, unemployment, inflation and growth. Both rest on the same three words: scarcity, choice, cost.

spotlights.name: Lionel Robbins and the definition
spotlights.spot_it: The LSE professor whose one sentence, 'ends and scarce means which have alternative uses', opens almost every economics textbook.
spotlights.story_md: Robbins was 33 when he published *An Essay on the Nature and Significance of Economic Science* in 1932. Before him, economics was often defined by its topics: wealth, trade, money. Robbins defined it by a **problem** instead. Anything where limited means meet competing ends is economic, whether it is a nation's steel or a student's evening. He also clashed with Keynes in 1930, refusing to sign a report that endorsed tariffs and walking out of the committee. Later he chaired the 1963 **Robbins Report**, which expanded British universities on the principle that every qualified person who wants a place should get one.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His definition turned economics into a way of thinking that can be applied to anything scarce.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ends, scarce means, alternative uses: three conditions, one science.

spotlights.name: The first lesson of economics
spotlights.spot_it: A two-line maxim: the first lesson of economics is scarcity, the first lesson of politics is to ignore it.
spotlights.story_md: The economist **Thomas Sowell**, born in 1930 in North Carolina, put the subject in one sentence in his 1993 book *Is Reality Optional?*: there is never enough of anything to fully satisfy all those who want it. His punchline followed: the first lesson of politics is to disregard the first lesson of economics. You do not have to share Sowell's politics to see the point. Every promise of more schools, more roads, lower taxes and lower prices all at once hides a trade-off. The economist's habit is to ask the rude question: and what will we give up for it?
spotlights.why_it_matters: It names the tension between what voters want and what resources allow.
spotlights.memory_hook: Economics says 'not enough'; politics says 'for everyone'.

spotlights.name: Samuelson's Economics
spotlights.spot_it: A thick textbook with a plain cover that taught the post-war world to draw supply curves and production frontiers.
spotlights.story_md: Paul Samuelson's *Economics* first appeared in 1948 and ran to **19 editions**, the last in 2009. It sold more than **four million** copies in **41 languages**. Between 1961 and 1976 every edition sold over 300,000 copies. The book made the production possibilities frontier, the guns-and-butter curve you will meet below, the standard first picture of scarcity for generations of students, including many in India. Samuelson himself won the second economics Nobel, in 1970.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It fixed the way the world first meets scarcity: as a curve on a blackboard.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four million copies, one bent curve.

sections.title: Before the word: household, kingdom, world
sections.intro_md:
The word economics comes from the Greek *oikonomia*: **oikos**, the household, and **nemein**, to manage. For two thousand years the subject was literally household management, scaled up to estates and kingdoms.

Thinkers on several continents wrestled with scarcity long before anyone called it that. A Greek soldier-writer wrote a dialogue on running a farm. Indian treatises on statecraft set out how a king should tax, store grain and fix wages. A North African historian noticed that tax rates and tax revenue do not rise together. A French court physician drew the first diagram of money flowing through a whole economy, like blood through a body.

What changed in the 18th century was the shift from **managing** scarce resources to **explaining** how millions of strangers allocate them without anyone in charge. That is the leap Adam Smith made, and it is why the timeline below speeds up after 1750.

spotlights.name: Xenophon's Oeconomicus
spotlights.spot_it: A Socratic dialogue about a gentleman farmer, his wife and his storerooms: the book that may have given us the word economy.
spotlights.story_md: Xenophon, a pupil of Socrates and a mercenary general, wrote the **Oeconomicus** late in life. Most of it is Socrates retelling a talk with **Ischomachus**, an Athenian landowner who explains how he trained his young wife to run the house, kept stores in order, managed slaves and farmed. It reads more like a manual than a theory. But it treats wealth as something produced by good management of limited land, labour and goods, and some philologists trace the very word *economy* to it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the oldest surviving works that treats managing scarce resources as a skill to be taught.
spotlights.memory_hook: Economics began as a lecture on keeping the pantry tidy.

spotlights.name: The Arthashastra
spotlights.spot_it: Palm-leaf bundles in Grantha script, lost for centuries, found in 1905 and read by a librarian in Mysore.
spotlights.story_md: The Arthashastra, compiled under the name **Kautilya** or Vishnugupta, is a Sanskrit treatise on statecraft in **15 books and 150 chapters**. It names *varta*, meaning agriculture, cattle and trade, as one of the four core fields of knowledge, and its longest book details the duties of superintendents of granaries, mints, mines, markets and weights. The text had dropped out of sight until **1905**, when a palm-leaf copy from Thanjavur reached the Mysore Oriental Library and its librarian **R. Shamasastry** recognised it. He published it in 1909. Tradition links Kautilya to Chanakya, Chandragupta Maurya's adviser, but most scholars since 1965 doubt that identification and date the final text to the early centuries CE.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows Indian thinkers treating taxation, storage and trade as a science of scarce state resources.
spotlights.memory_hook: A lost economics manual, rescued from a stack of palm leaves.

spotlights.name: Ibn Khaldun
spotlights.spot_it: A 14th-century North African historian whose Muqaddimah noticed that low tax rates can bring in more revenue than high ones.
spotlights.story_md: Ibn Khaldun, born in Tunis in 1332, finished the **Muqaddimah**, the introduction to his universal history, in 1377. Among its observations on cities, trade and the rise and fall of dynasties is one modern economists like to quote: early in a dynasty, taxes are light and bring in large revenue; late in a dynasty, rates rise but revenue falls, because heavy taxes kill the incentive to work and trade. The American economist Arthur Laffer later credited him for the idea behind the Laffer curve. He also wrote about the division of labour and prices centuries before Smith.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He saw that people respond to incentives, so a ruler's resources are not a fixed pie.
spotlights.memory_hook: Squeeze the camel too hard and it stops carrying.

spotlights.name: Quesnay's Tableau économique
spotlights.spot_it: A zigzag chart of money and produce moving between farmers, landlords and artisans, drawn by a royal doctor.
spotlights.story_md: **François Quesnay** was physician at the court of Louis XV. Perhaps because he knew how blood circulates, he pictured the economy as a **circular flow**. His Tableau économique of 1758 traces each year's harvest as it passes from farmers to landlords as rent, to artisans for goods, and back to farmers. Quesnay and his followers, the Physiocrats, wrongly believed only land produced a true surplus. But the Tableau was the first attempt to show a whole economy as an interlocking system, the ancestor of every macroeconomic model, including the water machine you will meet later.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the first picture of an economy as a system rather than a collection of households.
spotlights.memory_hook: A doctor drew the economy's bloodstream.

sections.title: Smith, Malthus, Ricardo: the classical answer
sections.intro_md:
The classical economists asked how a society with no central planner feeds itself, and what limits its growth.

**Adam Smith** answered the first question in 1776: specialise, trade, and let prices guide effort. Splitting work into narrow tasks makes each worker vastly more productive, and markets connect the specialists. **Thomas Malthus** answered the second question gloomily in 1798: population tends to grow faster than food, so most people will be pushed back to subsistence. **David Ricardo** in 1817 showed why two countries gain from trade even when one is better at everything, because what matters is not absolute skill but **opportunity cost**.

All three were thinking about scarcity. Smith saw how specialisation stretches scarce labour. Malthus saw land as the binding limit. Ricardo saw that every hour spent making one thing is an hour not spent on another, and built a theory of trade on that trade-off.

spotlights.name: Adam Smith and the pin factory
spotlights.spot_it: A Scottish professor in a wig whose book opens not with gold or kings but with a workshop making pins.
spotlights.story_md: *The Wealth of Nations* was published on **9 March 1776** and its first edition sold out in six months. Its first chapter describes a pin workshop where the job is split into about **18 operations**. Ten workers, each doing a few steps, could make about **48,000 pins a day**; one worker alone might struggle to make 20. That is the magic of the **division of labour**: the same scarce hours produce far more. The famous phrase **invisible hand** appears just once in the whole book, in Book IV. Smith's subject was less 'greed is good' than how specialisation and exchange stretch scarce means.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It founded economics as the study of how markets coordinate scarce labour without a boss.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ten people, eighteen steps, forty-eight thousand pins.

spotlights.name: Thomas Malthus and the population trap
spotlights.spot_it: An English clergyman's anonymous essay: population grows exponentially, food only arithmetically.
spotlights.story_md: Malthus published *An Essay on the Principle of Population* anonymously in **1798**. His argument: food production grows step by step while population, unchecked, multiplies. So hunger, disease and war, or later marriage and fewer births, must keep numbers in line with food. In 1805 he became professor of history and political economy at the **East India Company College** in Hertfordshire, training future officials of British India. His forecast failed for two centuries because farming technology and falling birth rates outran his arithmetic. Yet his core idea, that a fixed resource like land can cap living standards, still shapes debates about water, soil and climate.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He made the limits of natural resources a central question of economics.
spotlights.memory_hook: Malthus bet against the plough, and the plough kept winning.

spotlights.name: Ricardo's comparative advantage
spotlights.spot_it: Wine and cloth, Portugal and England: the example that shows trade helps even the country that is worse at everything.
spotlights.story_md: **David Ricardo**, a London stockbroker who made a fortune before he turned to economics, set out the theory in *On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation* (1817). Suppose Portugal makes both wine and cloth with less labour than England. Should it make both? No. What matters is what each country gives up. If Portugal's edge is biggest in wine, it should make wine and buy cloth, while England makes cloth. Both end up with more of both. The logic is pure opportunity cost: every worker making cloth in Portugal is a worker not making wine.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the trade-off logic behind why nations, firms and people specialise.
spotlights.memory_hook: Be better at everything, still do only what you are best at.

compare.difference: Smith said trade pays when each country is better at something; Ricardo showed it pays even when one country is better at everything.

sections.title: Why water is cheap and diamonds are dear
sections.intro_md:
Adam Smith noticed a puzzle. Nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything. A diamond has scarcely any use, yet it can be exchanged for a great quantity of other goods. Philosophers back to Plato had circled this **paradox of value**.

The answer arrived almost a century later, in three countries at once. Around 1871 to 1874 **William Stanley Jevons** in England, **Carl Menger** in Austria and **Léon Walras** in Switzerland argued that value is decided **at the margin**: by the usefulness of the *next* unit, not the total usefulness of all units. Water is so plentiful that the next glass adds almost nothing. Diamonds are so scarce that the next one adds a lot.

This is the **marginal revolution**, and it is how economists still think about trade-offs. You almost never choose between all water and all diamonds. You choose whether one more hour of study is worth one less hour of sleep. **Alfred Marshall** then combined the marginal buyer and the marginal seller into the supply and demand diagram.

spotlights.name: The water and diamond paradox
spotlights.spot_it: Two objects side by side: a glass of water and a rough diamond, and the question of why their prices run backwards.
spotlights.story_md: In Book I of *The Wealth of Nations* Smith separated **value in use** from **value in exchange** and left the gap unexplained in any satisfying way; he leaned on the labour needed to get things. The marginalists solved it. The Austrian Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk told it with a farmer and five sacks of grain: one to live on, one for strength, one for poultry, one for spirits, one for parrots. Lose a sack and you give up the parrots, not your life. So each sack is worth only its **least important use**. In a desert the same logic flips: the next litre of water saves your life and outranks any diamond.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the cleanest demonstration that scarcity at the margin, not usefulness, sets value.
spotlights.memory_hook: Water saves your life, but the next glass only wets your shirt.

spotlights.name: William Stanley Jevons
spotlights.spot_it: A Victorian logician and economist who put marginal utility into equations and worried England would run out of coal.
spotlights.story_md: Jevons proposed his theory in an 1862 paper and set it out in *The Theory of Political Economy* in **1871**. Value, he wrote, depends entirely on utility, and utility on the last increment consumed. Earlier, in *The Coal Question* (1865), he made a startling observation: James Watt's more efficient steam engine had **increased** Britain's coal use, because cheaper power found many more uses. This **Jevons paradox** is back in the news: Microsoft's Satya Nadella invoked it in 2025 to argue that cheaper AI would mean far more AI use, not less.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He helped launch marginalism and spotted that efficiency can increase total demand for a scarce resource.
spotlights.memory_hook: Make coal go further and you burn more coal.

spotlights.name: Carl Menger
spotlights.spot_it: A bearded Viennese professor who founded the Austrian school with a book on why things have value.
spotlights.story_md: Menger's *Principles of Economics* appeared in **1871**, the same year as Jevons's book, with no mathematics at all. He argued that goods have value because people judge them able to satisfy needs, and that the value of each unit depends on the least important need it satisfies. He also explained how money could arise without any government: traders gradually settle on the most widely accepted good. His students, including **Friedrich von Wieser** and Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk, built the Austrian school on his work.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He showed that value lives in people's judgments about scarce goods, not in the goods themselves.
spotlights.memory_hook: Value is in the mind of the chooser.

spotlights.name: Léon Walras
spotlights.spot_it: A French economist in Lausanne who wrote the whole economy as a system of equations.
spotlights.story_md: Walras published the first part of *Elements of Pure Economics* in **1874** while a professor at the University of Lausanne. Where Jevons and Menger studied one buyer facing one good, Walras asked how **all** markets clear at once: the price of bread affects wages, which affect the price of cloth, and so on. His **general equilibrium** model, with an imaginary auctioneer calling out prices until every market balances, is the ancestor of modern models used by central banks. Joseph Schumpeter later called him the greatest of all economists.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He showed that scarcity in one market ripples through every other.
spotlights.memory_hook: One auctioneer, every price, all at once.

spotlights.name: Alfred Marshall's scissors
spotlights.spot_it: The Cambridge professor who drew two crossing lines, supply and demand, and compared them to the blades of scissors.
spotlights.story_md: Marshall's *Principles of Economics* (1890) became the dominant English textbook for a generation. He was the first to develop the standard **supply and demand graph**. Asking whether value is set by utility or by cost, he said it was like asking which blade of a pair of scissors cuts the paper. His wife **Mary Paley Marshall**, one of the first women students at Cambridge, co-wrote *The Economics of Industry* (1879); their marriage cost him his college fellowship. His advice to economists: translate your mathematics into English, then burn the mathematics. **Keynes** was his student.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His diagram is still the first tool anyone uses to see how scarcity becomes a price.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two blades, one cut: demand and supply.

sections.title: The cost of anything is what you give up
sections.intro_md:
The single most useful idea in this subject is **opportunity cost**: the value of the best alternative you give up when you choose. The cost of a film is not just the ticket. It is also the two hours you could have spent on something else, and whatever that would have been worth to you.

Opportunity cost explains why a free lunch is never free, why a broken window does not create wealth, and why a doctor who earns ₹5,000 an hour is right to pay someone to do her accounts even if she is faster at them. It is also strangely hard to apply. In a 2005 test at the main American economics conference, most professional economists got a simple opportunity cost question wrong.

The term itself is usually credited to the Austrian **Friedrich von Wieser**, whose 1914 book set out the idea of cost as the alternative forgone. The idea is older than the label: Bastiat's 'unseen' in 1850 is the same insight in a parable.

spotlights.name: Friedrich von Wieser
spotlights.spot_it: An Austrian baron and economist who named both marginal utility and opportunity cost.
spotlights.story_md: Wieser, born in Vienna in 1851, coined the German word **Grenznutzen**, which became the English 'marginal utility'. In *Natural Value* (1889) and *Social Economics* (1914) he argued that the true cost of producing anything is the value of the other goods the same resources could have made. That is the theory of **alternative cost**, and Wikipedia and most textbooks credit him with the term opportunity cost. He succeeded Menger at Vienna in 1903 and served as Austria's minister of commerce from 1917 to the end of the First World War, in 1918, as the empire collapsed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He made 'cost' mean the alternatives sacrificed, not the money paid.
spotlights.memory_hook: Cost is the road not taken, priced.

spotlights.name: There ain't no such thing as a free lunch
spotlights.spot_it: TANSTAAFL: a saloon custom turned into the most famous eight words in economics.
spotlights.story_md: American saloons once offered a **free lunch** to anyone who bought a drink. The food was salty, so you bought more drinks; the lunch was paid for after all. In 1873 a newspaper called free lunch one of the most expensive things in the city. The saying 'There is no such thing as free lunch' first appears in a Cleveland column in **1933**, in a fable titled 'Economics in Eight Words'. In **1938** a Birmingham paper gave it the familiar 'ain't'. **Robert Heinlein** made the acronym TANSTAAFL a theme of his 1966 novel *The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress*, and **Milton Friedman** used the phrase as a book title in 1975.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is opportunity cost in a pub: someone, somewhere, always pays.
spotlights.memory_hook: The lunch is free; the salt is not.

spotlights.name: Bastiat's broken window
spotlights.spot_it: A boy breaks a shopkeeper's window, and the town cheers the work it creates for the glazier.
spotlights.story_md: **Frédéric Bastiat**, a French economist and member of parliament, wrote *That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen* in **1850**, the year he died. In his parable, onlookers console a shopkeeper whose window is broken: at least the glazier gets work. Bastiat's reply: the glazier's six francs are **seen**; what is **not seen** is the pair of shoes or the book the shopkeeper would otherwise have bought. Destruction is not profit. Henry Hazlitt made the parable the core of *Economics in One Lesson* (1946). You will still hear the fallacy after every disaster and war: 'at least it will boost the economy'.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It trains the eye to look for the hidden alternative behind every visible gain.
spotlights.memory_hook: Count the shoes that were never bought.

spotlights.name: The Eric Clapton ticket test
spotlights.spot_it: A one-question quiz about a free concert ticket that stumped a room of professional economists.
spotlights.story_md: At the 2005 American Economic Association meetings, Paul Ferraro and Laura Taylor asked about 200 economists this: you win a free ticket to see **Eric Clapton**, which you cannot resell. Bob Dylan plays the same night; his ticket costs $40 and you would pay up to $50 to see him. What is the opportunity cost of seeing Clapton? The answer is **$10**: the $50 of value from Dylan minus the $40 you would have paid. Only about **22%** of economists chose it, fewer than would have picked it at random from four options. Students did even worse.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that knowing a concept and using it are different skills.
spotlights.memory_hook: Clapton is free; giving up Dylan costs ten dollars.

sections.title: Guns or butter: the frontier of the possible
sections.intro_md:
The standard picture of scarcity is the **production possibilities frontier**. Imagine an economy that can make only two things, guns and butter. Put all its workers and machines on guns and you get, say, 100 guns and no butter. Put them all on butter and you get 500 tonnes of butter and no guns. Mixes fall on a curve between.

Three lessons hide in that curve. Points **inside** it are waste: idle workers, unused factories. Points **outside** it are impossible with today's resources. And moving **along** it is a trade-off: more of one means less of the other. The curve usually bows outward, because the workers best at farming are the last to be moved to arms factories, so each extra gun costs more butter than the one before.

Growth means pushing the whole frontier outward: more workers, better machines, new ideas. That is why the 2025 Nobel prize went to economists of innovation. Without it, every gain is someone else's loss.

spotlights.name: Guns versus butter
spotlights.spot_it: Two words that stand for every choice between defence and daily life.
spotlights.story_md: The phrase appears in American newspapers around the **National Defense Act of 1916**. It became notorious in Nazi Germany. On 17 January **1936** Joseph Goebbels said Germany could do without butter but not without arms. That summer Hermann Göring told a crowd that guns would make the nation powerful while butter would only make people fat. The regime chose rearmament over consumption, and Germans lived with shortages of fats long before the war. The phrase became the textbook name for the production possibilities frontier because it is so concrete: steel can become a tank or a tractor, not both.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It makes the abstract frontier visible: national power is paid for at the breakfast table.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every tank is a tractor that was not built.

spotlights.name: Johnson's guns and butter
spotlights.spot_it: A Texan president who tried to fund a war in Vietnam and a war on poverty at the same time.
spotlights.story_md: **Lyndon B. Johnson** launched the **Great Society** programmes of the mid-1960s, including Medicare and the war on poverty, while escalating the war in Vietnam. He used the 'guns and butter' language himself, insisting America could afford both. Many economists argue the attempt to have both without raising taxes enough fed the inflation that began in the late 1960s and worsened through the 1970s. Wikipedia flags the direct link as needing a citation, so treat it as a common reading, not a settled verdict. It remains the classic warning that a frontier is a frontier even for a superpower.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that a rich country still faces the same trade-off as a poor one, just at larger numbers.
spotlights.memory_hook: Both guns and butter, paid for later with rising prices.

sections.title: The scarcest things are not things
sections.intro_md:
Money is the scarce resource people notice. Time and attention are the ones that run out first.

Everyone, rich or poor, gets **24 hours** a day. You cannot save time, borrow much of it or buy more of it, though you can buy other people's. In 1965 the economist **Gary Becker** argued that households are like small factories that combine purchased goods with their own time to produce what they really want: meals, rest, children, fun. That is why richer people, whose hours are worth more in wages, buy ready meals and taxis and why chores move to machines as wages rise.

Attention is time's sharper cousin. In 1971 **Herbert Simon** wrote that a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention. The whole business model of social media sits on that sentence: the product is free because you pay with the scarce thing. And in 1930 **John Maynard Keynes** predicted that his grandchildren would be so rich they would work about **15 hours a week**. Output grew roughly as he forecast; the free time did not arrive.

spotlights.name: Franklin's daily schedule
spotlights.spot_it: A handwritten grid with every hour of one day assigned: rise at five, work, read, sleep at ten.
spotlights.story_md: In his autobiography **Benjamin Franklin** printed the timetable he drew up as a young printer in Philadelphia. It starts with a question for the morning, 'What good shall I do this day?', and ends with another at night. Between them, every block of the 24 hours is assigned: work, meals, reading, music, sleep. Franklin also wrote, in 1748, that **time is money**. An economist would refine that: time is the scarce means behind all others, and its price is whatever you would have earned or enjoyed in the next best use.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a historical record of someone treating hours as a budget to allocate.
spotlights.memory_hook: A budget, but in hours: you never get a refund.

spotlights.name: Gary Becker's economics of time
spotlights.spot_it: A Chicago economist who applied price theory to marriage, crime, children and the hours in a day.
spotlights.story_md: Gary Becker won the 1992 Nobel prize for extending economic reasoning to almost all human behaviour. His 1965 paper *A Theory of the Allocation of Time* treated the family as a producer combining goods and time. A home-cooked dinner uses cheap ingredients and expensive hours; a restaurant meal uses expensive goods and few hours. As wages rise, the hour becomes the dearer input, so people shift towards time-saving goods. That simple shift helps explain the spread of washing machines, ready meals and food delivery apps, including India's Swiggy and Zomato boom.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It made time the hidden price inside every consumer choice.
spotlights.memory_hook: When your hour gets dearer, the dinner gets delivered.

spotlights.name: Herbert Simon's poverty of attention
spotlights.spot_it: A Nobel economist and AI pioneer's one-line warning about the information age, written before the personal computer.
spotlights.story_md: **Herbert Simon** won the 1975 Turing Award for work on artificial intelligence and the 1978 Nobel prize in economics for research on decision-making. He argued that people are **boundedly rational**: they cannot weigh every option, so they **satisfice**, picking the first option that is good enough. In a 1971 essay, *Designing Organizations for an Information-Rich World*, he wrote that information consumes the attention of its recipients, hence a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention. Half a century later, platforms compete for that scarce attention every second.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It identified attention as the bottleneck of the information age.
spotlights.memory_hook: More to read, less of you to read it.

spotlights.name: Keynes's letter to his grandchildren
spotlights.spot_it: A short 1930 essay predicting that by 2030 the economic problem of scarcity might be solved.
spotlights.story_md: In the depths of the Depression, **John Maynard Keynes** wrote *Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren*. He forecast that in a hundred years living standards in progressive countries would be **four to eight times** higher, and that people might need to work only about **three hours a day**, a 15-hour week. The economic problem, the struggle for subsistence, would be on its way to solution, leaving the harder problem of how to live wisely. He got the growth roughly right for rich countries. He got the leisure wrong: wants kept growing faster than needs, and scarcity moved from bread to time, status and attention.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most famous bet that scarcity would end, and the clearest evidence of how wants grow.
spotlights.memory_hook: Keynes promised a 15-hour week; we took the extra stuff instead.

sections.title: What scarcity does to a mind
sections.intro_md:
Economics long assumed that people facing scarcity simply choose more carefully. Psychology suggests scarcity also changes **how** people think.

The Harvard economist **Sendhil Mullainathan** and Princeton psychologist **Eldar Shafir** call it **tunnelling**. When you are short of money, time or food, the shortage captures your attention. You focus hard on the immediate gap, which helps meet a deadline, but everything outside the tunnel gets neglected. They describe a **bandwidth tax**: worry about scarcity uses up mental capacity that would otherwise go to planning, patience and self-control.

The evidence comes from very different places: young men starving on purpose in a Minnesota stadium in 1944, sugarcane farmers in Tamil Nadu tested before and after harvest, and shoppers asked to think about a car repair bill. It also comes with a warning. Some famous findings in this area, like the marshmallow test, look weaker on replication than they did in the headlines.

spotlights.name: The Minnesota Starvation Experiment
spotlights.spot_it: Thirty-six thin volunteers in a university lab, obsessed with food, studied so aid workers would know how to refeed a starving Europe.
spotlights.story_md: From November 1944 to December 1945 the physiologist **Ancel Keys** ran a study at the University of Minnesota on **36 men**, conscientious objectors chosen from hundreds of volunteers. After 12 weeks on about 3,200 calories a day, they spent 24 weeks on about **1,560**, aiming to lose a quarter of their body weight. They became depressed, irritable and withdrawn, lost interest in sex and became **preoccupied with food**, talking and dreaming about it. The results filled the two-volume *Biology of Human Starvation* (1950), 1,385 pages, and early findings guided relief workers in post-war Europe and Asia.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed that scarcity takes over the mind, not just the body.
spotlights.memory_hook: Starve the body and the mind thinks only of bread.

spotlights.name: The sugarcane farmers of Tamil Nadu
spotlights.spot_it: The same farmers, tested twice: once when broke before the harvest, once flush after it.
spotlights.story_md: Sugarcane farmers in **Tamil Nadu** are paid once a year, when the cane is sold, so they are poor before harvest and comparatively rich after. In a study published in *Science* in 2013, **Anandi Mani, Sendhil Mullainathan, Eldar Shafir and Jiaying Zhao** gave the same farmers cognitive tests, including Raven's matrices and a Stroop test, before and after harvest. Before harvest they scored worse. Because the comparison is within the same people, it rules out the idea that poorer people are simply less able. The authors argue that money worry taxes mental bandwidth. Mullainathan himself was born in a farming village in Tamil Nadu.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It reframes poverty as a constant tax on attention, with implications for how welfare is designed.
spotlights.memory_hook: Same farmer, same brain, smaller bandwidth before payday.

spotlights.name: Scarcity, the book
spotlights.spot_it: A popular book with a simple claim: having too little of anything, money or time, narrows the mind in the same way.
spotlights.story_md: Mullainathan and Shafir published *Scarcity: Why Having Too Little Means So Much* in **2013**. Their striking move is to treat a busy executive with no time and a poor family with no money as facing the same mental trap. Both tunnel: they meet the immediate deadline, but borrow against the future, by taking a high-interest loan or skipping tomorrow's planning. The policy lesson is practical: make programmes for poor people simple, forgiving of missed deadlines, and light on paperwork, because every form costs scarce bandwidth.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It links the economics of scarcity to the psychology of decision-making.
spotlights.memory_hook: Short of money or short of time, you end up in the same tunnel.

spotlights.name: The marshmallow test, revisited
spotlights.spot_it: A child alone in a room with one treat now or two treats later, the most famous test of waiting.
spotlights.story_md: In Stanford experiments from 1970, **Walter Mischel** and colleagues offered preschoolers one treat now or two if they waited about 15 minutes. Follow-ups linked waiting longer to better SAT scores and outcomes. A 2012 Rochester study then showed children waited far less, about a quarter as long, after an adult broke a promise: waiting is a rational bet on whether the second treat will appear. A larger 2018 replication by **Watts, Duncan and Quan** found about half the original effect, mostly explained by family background. For a child who has learned that resources vanish, eating the treat now is sensible.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that apparent impatience can be a reasonable response to scarcity and unreliable promises.
spotlights.memory_hook: If the second marshmallow might never come, eat the first.

sections.title: Modelling scarcity, with water
sections.intro_md:
Economists cannot run a country twice, so they build **models**: simplified versions of the economy that keep the trade-offs and throw away the detail. The key phrase is **ceteris paribus**, 'other things equal': change one thing, hold the rest fixed, and see what happens.

Most models live in equations. One famous model lived in plumbing. In 1949 a New Zealand engineering student turned economist, **Bill Phillips**, built a machine in which coloured water stood for money. Tanks were savings and government coffers, pipes were spending and taxes, valves were policy. Pump in more water as government spending and you could watch income rise and then leak away into imports and savings.

The point of the machine is the same as the point of every model: money spent on one thing cannot be spent on another, and every flow must come from somewhere. Water makes scarcity visible.

spotlights.name: The MONIAC, or Phillips Machine
spotlights.spot_it: A two-metre cabinet of clear tanks and tubes in which coloured water flows like money through the British economy.
spotlights.story_md: Phillips built the first machine with fellow economist **Walter Newlyn** in his landlady's garage in Croydon, for about **£400**. It stood about **2 metres** tall. Water pumped to the top represented national income; it flowed down into consumption, taxes, savings and imports, with valves for interest rates and spending. Between **12 and 14** were built. Buyers included Harvard Business School and Melbourne University. Working machines survive at the Science Museum in London, at Cambridge and at the Reserve Bank of New Zealand museum. It was an analogue computer for economics before digital ones were common.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned the abstract circular flow of an economy into something students could watch leak.
spotlights.memory_hook: An economy you could drain with a spanner.

spotlights.name: Bill Phillips
spotlights.spot_it: A New Zealander who had been a crocodile hunter and a prisoner of war before he became an LSE professor.
spotlights.story_md: Alban William Housego Phillips was born near Dannevirke, New Zealand, in **1914**. In Australia he worked as a **crocodile hunter** and cinema manager. In the Second World War he was captured in Java and spent three and a half years in a Japanese camp, where he learned Chinese and secretly repaired and miniaturised a radio. He became an MBE in 1946. At the LSE he built the MONIAC, became a professor in 1958 and, the same year, published the paper on unemployment and wage growth that became the **Phillips curve**, one of the most argued-over graphs in macroeconomics.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His life is a reminder that economics was built by tinkerers as well as theorists.
spotlights.memory_hook: From crocodiles to curves, by way of a secret radio.

sections.title: Who gets what: price, queue, ration, lottery, match
sections.intro_md:
Scarcity means something must decide who gets the scarce thing. There are only a handful of ways to do it, and every society uses all of them.

**Price**: whoever pays most gets it. Efficient at matching goods to those who value them, harsh on those who cannot pay. **Queue**: first come, first served. Fair in one sense, but people pay with hours instead of money. **Ration**: a fixed share for each, by rule. Used in wartime Britain and in India's ration shops. **Lottery**: chance decides, as in some visa and licence systems. **Need or merit**: an authority judges, as with school seats or hospital triage. **Matching**: clever design pairs people when money is banned, as with kidney exchanges. **Community rules**: users of a shared resource set and police their own limits, which is what Elinor Ostrom found working from Swiss meadows to Nepal's canals.

No method abolishes scarcity. Each one just chooses who bears it, and how.

visual.title: Ways to allocate a scarce thing

data.Who pays the cost: Those who want more than the share

spotlights.name: The Soviet queue
spotlights.spot_it: Long lines of coats outside a bread shop: shoppers paying in hours because prices were fixed below what the market would bear.
spotlights.story_md: When prices are held low and supply does not keep up, goods are allocated by **queue**. In the Soviet Union people sometimes spent hours a day in lines for basic food, and in the 1980s the wait for an apartment could last **10 to 15 years**. The Hungarian economist **János Kornai** argued in *Economics of Shortage* (1980) that this was not bad planning but a built-in flaw. State firms faced a **soft budget constraint**: losses would be covered, so they never had to economise, and demand for inputs was endless. Shortage was the normal state, not the exception.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that abolishing high prices does not abolish scarcity; it changes the currency to time.
spotlights.memory_hook: No price tag, so you pay in hours.

spotlights.name: Britain's ration book
spotlights.spot_it: A small buff booklet of coupons, stamped by the grocer for each week's tea, sugar, fat and bacon.
spotlights.story_md: Britain rationed **bacon, butter and sugar** from 8 January 1940; by August 1942 almost everything except vegetables and bread was on the ration. Bread itself was only rationed **after** the war, from 1946 to 1948. Sweets came off the ration in 1949, went back on, and were finally freed in 1953. Food rationing ended on **4 July 1954**, with meat. Surprisingly, public health improved: infant mortality fell and life expectancy rose, because everyone got a fixed share of protein and vitamins.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the textbook case of allocating scarcity by equal shares instead of by wallet.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fourteen years of coupons, and a healthier nation at the end.

spotlights.name: India's ration shops
spotlights.spot_it: A small fair price shop with a queue at its window, ration cards in hand, sacks of rice and wheat inside.
spotlights.story_md: India's **Public Distribution System** grew from wartime rationing after the Bengal famine. The **National Food Security Act, 2013** entitled up to 75% of rural and 50% of urban people, about **two-thirds** of the country, to **5 kg** of grain per person per month at ₹3 for rice, ₹2 for wheat and ₹1 for coarse grains. Since the pandemic, grain under the PMGKAY scheme has been free; in 2023 the Centre extended free grain for five years from **January 2024 to December 2028**, covering about **81.35 crore** people at an estimated ₹11.8 lakh crore. It is the largest food ration system in the world.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Sen's entitlement idea turned into policy: a legal claim on food, independent of the market price.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five kilos a month, by law, for two Indians in three.

spotlights.name: Kidney exchange: allocating without prices
spotlights.spot_it: Chains of strangers giving kidneys to strangers, so each donor's loved one gets a matching kidney from someone else.
spotlights.story_md: Buying and selling organs is banned in most countries, so price cannot ration kidneys. Many patients have a willing donor whose kidney does not match. The fix is a **swap**: donor A gives to patient B, donor B gives to patient A. The first recorded paired exchanges were in **South Korea in 1991**. The economist **Alvin Roth** helped design matching algorithms that string swaps into long chains; one 2014 American chain had **70 participants**. Roth shared the 2012 Nobel prize for this kind of **market design**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows economics allocating a scarce good fairly when money is ruled out.
spotlights.memory_hook: No price, no queue jumping: just a very clever swap.

spotlights.name: Elinor Ostrom and the commons
spotlights.spot_it: The first woman to win the economics Nobel, a political scientist who studied fishermen, herders and irrigators.
spotlights.story_md: A common, like a fishery or pasture, is a scarce resource no one owns outright. The biologist Garrett Hardin argued in 1968 that such resources are doomed to overuse: the **tragedy of the commons**. **Elinor Ostrom** looked at real communities and found many that had run commons well for centuries: alpine pastures in Switzerland and Japan, irrigation in Spain, the Philippines and **Nepal**, fisheries in Nova Scotia. In *Governing the Commons* (1990) she set out **eight design principles**, including clear boundaries, graduated sanctions and cheap conflict resolution. She won the Nobel in **2009**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She showed scarcity can be managed by communities, not only by markets or the state.
spotlights.memory_hook: The commons is not a tragedy if the commoners write the rules.

sections.title: Are we running out? The great wager
sections.intro_md:
Since Malthus, one argument has never quite ended. One side says resources are finite and growth will hit a wall. The other says scarcity drives up prices, prices drive invention and substitution, and humanity keeps finding more.

In 1980 the argument turned into a bet. The biologist **Paul Ehrlich**, author of the 1968 bestseller *The Population Bomb*, took up a challenge from the economist **Julian Simon**. Simon won, and the story is often told as a knockout. The fuller story is more interesting: Simon was partly lucky in his decade, and both sides could point to evidence.

India's own history adds another chapter. In the mid-1960s the country depended on American grain shipments and was widely expected to face mass famine. Instead, new seeds, fertiliser and irrigation, the **Green Revolution**, pushed the food frontier outward. The bill came later, in the falling water tables of Punjab.

visual.title: Two of the five metals in Simon and Ehrlich's bet (US$ per pound)

spotlights.name: The Simon and Ehrlich wager
spotlights.spot_it: A $1,000 bet on five metals, settled by a cheque for $576.07 in the post.
spotlights.story_md: On **29 September 1980** Ehrlich and two colleagues chose five metals: **copper, chromium, nickel, tin and tungsten**, and notionally bought $200 of each. If their inflation-adjusted prices rose by 1990, Simon would pay the difference; if they fell, Ehrlich would. Tin fell from $8.72 to $3.88 a pound. In October 1990 Ehrlich mailed Simon a cheque for **$576.07**. Later studies are less tidy: one found that across all decades from 1900 to 2008 Simon would have won only **38.4%** of the time, and Jeremy Grantham found that over 1980 to 2011 he would have lost on four of the five metals.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most famous test of whether scarcity tightens or loosens over time.
spotlights.memory_hook: A doom-monger paid $576.07 to an optimist, and the argument went on.

spotlights.name: India's Green Revolution
spotlights.spot_it: Short, stiff, high-yielding wheat standing in irrigated Punjab fields where famine had been forecast.
spotlights.story_md: In the mid-1960s, after droughts, India relied heavily on imported American grain. Agricultural scientist **M. S. Swaminathan**, working with **Norman Borlaug**'s high-yielding dwarf wheat from Mexico, led the push to plant new seeds with fertiliser and assured irrigation, starting in **Punjab** in 1966 to 1967. By 1970 Punjab was producing a large share of India's food grain. The frontier moved outward. But the trade-offs moved too: heavy fertiliser and pesticide use, soil damage, debt for small farmers, and groundwater pumped faster than rain could refill it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the strongest Indian case that technology can loosen scarcity, and a warning that it shifts costs elsewhere.
spotlights.memory_hook: New seeds beat the famine forecast; the water table paid the bill.

spotlights.name: The Jevons paradox
spotlights.spot_it: Efficiency that saves a resource per use but increases its total use.
spotlights.story_md: Jevons's 1865 observation about coal shows up wherever a scarce input gets cheaper to use. Cars with better mileage get driven more. Reservoirs built to end shortages invite more building and more water use, raising the risk of shortage again. Higher wheat yields can tempt farmers to plough more land, not less. The paradox does not always hold: farm productivity cut farm jobs because people did not want much more food. It matters today for **energy, water and AI**: in 2025 tech leaders, including Microsoft's Satya Nadella, argued that cheaper AI would raise total demand for computing.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It warns that efficiency alone does not end scarcity if demand expands to fill the gap.
spotlights.memory_hook: Better engines, more coal; cheaper AI, more chips.

sections.title: India's hardest trade-offs
sections.intro_md:
Every country's history can be read as a series of trade-offs under scarcity. India's are unusually sharp, because it has about 18% of the world's people on a much smaller share of its land and water.

In 1956 India chose **steel over consumer goods**, betting that heavy industry today would mean more of everything tomorrow. In 1991, with foreign exchange for about **three weeks of imports**, it pledged its **gold** to borrow dollars. In 2019 Chennai, a city of millions, ran out of reservoir water. Each year the Union budget forces the same choice in public: a rupee spent on defence cannot also build a rural road or fund a school.

The India connection runs the other way too. Indian economists have shaped how the world thinks about scarcity: Mahalanobis on planning, Sen on famine and entitlements, Mullainathan on the psychology of scarcity, and **Abhijit Banerjee**, who shared the 2019 Nobel with **Esther Duflo** and Michael Kremer for testing anti-poverty ideas with randomised trials, many of them in India.

visual.title: Indian economists who reshaped the study of scarcity

spotlights.name: The Mahalanobis plan
spotlights.spot_it: A physicist-statistician's model that told Nehru's India to build machines that make machines.
spotlights.story_md: **P. C. Mahalanobis**, founder of the Indian Statistical Institute in Kolkata, built the model behind India's **Second Five-Year Plan** (1956 to 1961) at Nehru's request. The trade-off was explicit: put scarce investment into **capital goods**, steel, machinery, power, rather than consumer goods. Growth would be slower at first and consumption would stay low, but the economy would grow faster later. Within two years the plan hit inflation and a foreign exchange crunch and was modified in 1958. Economists still argue whether the bet built India's industrial base or starved its farms and factories of simpler goods.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is India's clearest national choice between consumption now and capacity later.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fewer shirts now, more steel mills for later.

spotlights.name: When India flew its gold to London
spotlights.spot_it: Chartered planes, secret cargo, and 47 tonnes of the Reserve Bank's gold landing at the Bank of England.
spotlights.story_md: By mid-1991 India's foreign exchange reserves had fallen to roughly what would pay for **three weeks** of essential imports, and default was weeks away. Between 21 and 31 May, during a general election, the Reserve Bank of India secretly airlifted **47 tonnes** of gold to the **Bank of England** and **20 tonnes** to the Union Bank of Switzerland as collateral, raising about $600 million. When the news broke there was public outrage. In July the new finance minister, **Manmohan Singh**, devalued the rupee and presented the reform budget of 24 July 1991. In 2024 the RBI brought 100 tonnes of gold home from the UK.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the moment scarcity of dollars forced India to rethink its entire economic model.
spotlights.memory_hook: Gold went out on a plane; liberalisation came back.

spotlights.name: Chennai's Day Zero
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of coloured plastic pots at a tap, and four lakes reduced to cracked mud.
spotlights.story_md: On **19 June 2019** officials declared Day Zero in Chennai. The city's four main reservoirs, **Red Hills, Cholavaram, Poondi and Chembarambakkam**, had fallen to about 0.1% of capacity. About 11 million residents had no piped drinking water; tankers could not reach many slum residents; a special train carried water into the city. The causes were human as well as natural: a monsoon 55% short in 2018, a heatwave, sewage-polluted lakes, building on catchments, and groundwater pumped at twice the recharge rate. Water is cheap in Chennai until, at the margin, it is priceless.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the paradox of value in a real Indian city: the cheapest resource becomes the scarcest.
spotlights.memory_hook: Water was worthless until the taps ran dry.

spotlights.name: The 2026-27 Union budget
spotlights.spot_it: A finance minister's speech and a thick set of tables that say, rupee by rupee, what India chose.
spotlights.story_md: **Nirmala Sitharaman** presented India's 2026-27 budget on **1 February 2026**. It plans spending of about **₹53.5 lakh crore** against revenue of about ₹36.5 lakh crore, and a fiscal deficit of **4.3% of GDP**, with public debt around 55.6% of GDP. Every budget is a production possibilities frontier in prose: more for defence or roads means less elsewhere, or more borrowing, which shifts the cost to future taxpayers. In September 2025 the government had also cut GST to two main rates, **5% and 18%**, betting that lower taxes would raise spending enough to soften the loss of revenue.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the yearly public record of a nation's trade-offs.
spotlights.memory_hook: A budget is a list of everything you chose not to buy.

sections.title: Myths and misreadings
sections.intro_md:
Scarcity is one of the most misunderstood ideas in public debate. A few corrections worth carrying around:

**Myth: economics is about money.** It is about choice under scarcity. Money is just one scarce means, and often not the scarcest.

**Myth: scarcity means poverty.** Scarcity is universal; poverty is having too little to meet basic needs. A billionaire faces scarcity of time. A rich country faces guns and butter.

**Myth: a shortage and scarcity are the same thing.** A **shortage** is a specific market failure to clear: more people want a good at the going price than there are goods, usually because the price is held down. Raise the price and the shortage can vanish. Scarcity never vanishes.

**Myth: 'free' things cost nothing.** Free apps cost attention; free healthcare costs taxes and waiting time; free grain costs the public purse.

And two misquotations and a scare story that are worth checking before you repeat them.

spotlights.name: Why economics is called the dismal science
spotlights.spot_it: A famous insult usually blamed on Malthus's gloom, which actually came from a defence of forced labour.
spotlights.story_md: Most people assume 'the dismal science' describes Malthus's grim forecasts. The phrase was coined by the Scottish writer **Thomas Carlyle** in **1849**, in an essay later titled *Occasional Discourse on the Negro Question*. Carlyle attacked economists such as John Stuart Mill who supported the emancipation of enslaved people in the West Indies and who thought markets and free labour should replace coercion. Carlyle wanted a return to forced labour. So the insult was aimed at economists for being too committed to human freedom, not too gloomy about food.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a reminder to check the origin of a phrase before using it as an argument.
spotlights.memory_hook: Dismal, said the man who missed slavery.

spotlights.name: Shortage is not scarcity
spotlights.spot_it: A grand Moscow shopping arcade, short of goods in a country rich in land, oil and timber.
spotlights.story_md: The Soviet Union had vast resources, so it was not short of means in the Robbins sense more than other countries. Yet its shops were famous for empty shelves. That is the difference: **scarcity** is the gap between wants and means everywhere; **shortage** is what happens when prices are not allowed to move and supply does not respond. Rent control can create a housing shortage in a city with plenty of buildings. A fixed festival-season train fare creates a ticket shortage on routes that have seats in other weeks. Fix the shortage and scarcity remains, but people stop queueing.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Confusing the two leads to bad policy: blaming nature for problems made by rules.
spotlights.memory_hook: Scarcity is nature's rule; shortage is a price that cannot move.

spotlights.name: The '21 cities run dry by 2020' warning
spotlights.spot_it: A widely shared headline that Delhi, Bengaluru, Chennai and others would run out of groundwater by 2020.
spotlights.story_md: A June 2018 **NITI Aayog** report projected that at least **21 major Indian cities**, including New Delhi, Bengaluru and Hyderabad, would run out of groundwater by **2020**. The line was repeated across Indian and world media. The deadline passed and the cities did not run dry; Bengaluru's groundwater levels even recovered in 2021 after good rains. That does not mean the problem was invented: long-term declines are real, and Chennai did face Day Zero in 2019. It means alarming forecasts should be read for the trend they describe, not the date they promise.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Overstated deadlines can make real scarcity easier to dismiss.
spotlights.memory_hook: The date was wrong; the falling water table is not.

sections.title: Scarcity now: 2025 to 2026
sections.intro_md:
Scarcity in the news today is less about bread and more about chips, minerals and ideas.

The AI boom has created a **memory chip shortage**. DRAM prices reportedly rose about 172% during 2025 as manufacturers diverted capacity to high-bandwidth memory for AI servers. By 2026 memory made up about 35% of HP's PC materials cost, and analysts forecast PC shipments falling about 10%. **Rare earths**, used in the magnets of electric cars, wind turbines and missiles, are mined and especially refined mostly in China, which tightened export controls in April and October 2025 before suspending the second round for a year.

Meanwhile the economics prize has gone to the economists of **growth**, the force that pushes the scarcity frontier outward. The 2025 prize went to **Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt** for explaining innovation-driven growth. The 2026 prize, announced in October, went to the macroeconomists **Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford**.

spotlights.name: The AI memory chip squeeze
spotlights.spot_it: A memory chip die under a microscope: the component whose price doubled because AI servers wanted it more than laptops did.
spotlights.story_md: Chipmakers cut output in the 2022 to 2023 slump. Then AI demand for **high-bandwidth memory** soared. Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron shifted wafers to HBM, squeezing ordinary DRAM. In October 2025 OpenAI signed letters of intent with Samsung and SK Hynix that reports said could require up to 900,000 wafers a month, about **40% of global DRAM output**. Late in 2025 Micron announced it would leave its Crucial consumer business. In 2026 Apple raised some prices and SK Group's chairman predicted the shortage could last until **2030**. This is opportunity cost at industrial scale: every wafer for AI is a wafer not used in phones and PCs.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a live case of one booming use bidding a scarce input away from all others.
spotlights.memory_hook: AI ate the RAM, so your laptop costs more.

spotlights.name: Rare earths and China's leverage
spotlights.spot_it: Pale ore from a vast desert mine in Inner Mongolia, ending as a shiny magnet in a car motor or a fighter jet.
spotlights.story_md: Rare earths are not very rare in the ground; what is scarce is the capacity to **separate and refine** them. China does about **91%** of the world's rare earth separation and refining and makes about **94%** of sintered permanent magnets, according to IEA figures for 2024. On **4 April 2025**, responding to US tariffs, it restricted exports of heavy rare earths; in **October 2025** it broadened controls to materials for defence and chips. The second wave was then suspended for a year and general licences were issued for civilian trade. India, Japan, the US and Europe are now paying to build refining capacity of their own.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that scarcity can be created by control of a bottleneck, not only by nature.
spotlights.memory_hook: The rock is common; the refinery is rare.

spotlights.name: The 2025 Nobel: growth beats scarcity
spotlights.spot_it: Three economists honoured for explaining why, since about 1800, the frontier keeps moving outward.
spotlights.story_md: For most of history, living standards barely rose. Then, from the Industrial Revolution, growth became normal. Half the 2025 prize went to economic historian **Joel Mokyr**, born in Leiden in 1946 and raised in Haifa, for identifying the prerequisites for **sustained growth through technological progress**: a culture that values useful knowledge and is open to change. The other half went to **Philippe Aghion** and **Peter Howitt**, whose 1992 model formalised **creative destruction**: new firms and ideas replace old ones. Their work is a reply to Malthus. Scarcity does not go away, but the means grow faster than the mouths.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It honours the only lasting answer to scarcity: producing more with the same resources.
spotlights.memory_hook: You cannot beat scarcity, but you can outgrow it.

sections.title: Ten ideas to keep
sections.intro_md:
1. **Scarcity** means wants exceed means. It is universal and permanent; poverty is something else.
2. Robbins (1932): economics studies behaviour as a relationship between **ends and scarce means with alternative uses**.
3. Every choice has an **opportunity cost**: the best alternative given up. Clapton is free; Dylan is not.
4. Value is set **at the margin**, which is why water is cheap and diamonds dear until you are in a desert or in Chennai in June 2019.
5. The **production possibilities frontier** shows trade-offs: inside is waste, outside is impossible, along it is choice. Growth pushes it out.
6. **Time and attention** are the scarcest means of all, and scarcity itself taxes mental bandwidth.
7. Every society allocates scarce things by **price, queue, ration, lottery, need, matching or community rules**. None abolishes scarcity; each chooses who bears it.
8. A **shortage** is a price that cannot move; **scarcity** is the human condition.
9. Famine is about **entitlements** as well as food: Bengal 1943 had more rice than 1941.
10. The long-run answer is **innovation**, the subject of the 2025 Nobel. Scarcity stays; the frontier moves.

cards.front: Robbins's 1932 definition of economics, in three key phrases?
cards.back: The study of behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have alternative uses.

cards.front: What is opportunity cost?
cards.back: The value of the best alternative you give up when you make a choice.

cards.front: Scarcity vs shortage?
cards.back: Scarcity: wants exceed means, always and everywhere. Shortage: at the going price more is wanted than supplied, usually because the price cannot rise.

cards.front: Why is water cheap and diamonds dear?
cards.back: Value is set at the margin. Water is plentiful, so the next unit adds little; diamonds are scarce, so the next one adds a lot.

cards.front: Which three economists launched the marginal revolution, and when?
cards.back: Jevons (England, 1871), Menger (Austria, 1871), Walras (Switzerland, 1874).

cards.front: Clapton ticket test: what is the opportunity cost of the free Clapton ticket?
cards.back: $10: the $50 you would pay to see Dylan minus his $40 ticket price. Only about 22% of economists got it.

cards.front: What do points inside, on and outside a production possibilities frontier mean?
cards.back: Inside: waste. On: efficient, a trade-off. Outside: impossible with current resources.

cards.front: Bengal 1943: rice supply compared with 1941?
cards.back: About 13% higher, yet famine killed around 2.1 million.

cards.front: Sen's key word for what a person can command, through what they own, earn or receive?
cards.back: Entitlement.

cards.front: Who is this economist, and what did he show about famines?
cards.back: Amartya Sen: famines can happen when food exists but people's entitlements to it collapse.

cards.front: Origin of the word economics?
cards.back: Greek oikonomia: oikos (household) + nemein (to manage). Household management.

cards.front: The Arthashastra: how many books, and when was it rediscovered?
cards.back: 15 books, 150 chapters; a palm-leaf copy was identified at the Mysore Oriental Library in 1905.

cards.front: Smith's pin workshop: how many pins could ten workers make a day?
cards.back: About 48,000, by splitting the job into about 18 operations.

cards.front: Why should Portugal make wine and buy cloth even if it makes both more cheaply than England?
cards.back: Comparative advantage: what matters is opportunity cost. Specialising where your relative edge is largest leaves both countries with more.

cards.front: Name this machine and what the water stands for.
cards.back: The MONIAC or Phillips Machine (1949). The water is money flowing through the economy.

cards.front: Who coined 'the dismal science', when, and in what context?
cards.back: Thomas Carlyle, 1849, attacking economists who supported the emancipation of enslaved people.

cards.front: The Simon-Ehrlich bet: which metals, and who won?
cards.back: Copper, chromium, nickel, tin, tungsten. Simon won; Ehrlich paid $576.07 in 1990.

cards.front: 1991: how much gold did India send to the Bank of England?
cards.back: 47 tonnes (plus 20 tonnes to Union Bank of Switzerland), in May 1991.

cards.front: Mullainathan and Shafir: what are tunnelling and the bandwidth tax?
cards.back: Scarcity narrows focus to the immediate gap (tunnelling) and uses up mental capacity for everything else (bandwidth tax).

cards.front: Who won the 2025 economics Nobel, and for what?
cards.back: Joel Mokyr (half), Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt: innovation-driven growth and creative destruction.

cards.front: Who is this, and what idea did he put in one sentence in 1932?
cards.back: Lionel Robbins: economics as the study of ends and scarce means with alternative uses.

cards.front: Name this Scottish author and his 1776 book.
cards.back: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations.

cards.front: Who is this clergyman, and what did his 1798 essay claim?
cards.back: Thomas Malthus: population tends to outgrow food, keeping most people near subsistence.

cards.front: Who drew the supply and demand 'scissors'?
cards.back: Alfred Marshall, Principles of Economics, 1890.

cards.front: This French writer's parable is about a broken window. Who is he and what is the lesson?
cards.back: Frédéric Bastiat (1850): count what is not seen; destruction is not profit.

cards.front: Who is she, and what did she show about the commons?
cards.back: Elinor Ostrom: communities can manage shared resources with their own rules. First woman economics laureate, 2009.

cards.front: What is happening in this wartime British photograph?
cards.back: A grocer stamps a ration book: food allocated by fixed shares, 1940 to 1954.

cards.front: Which Chennai lake is this, and what happened in June 2019?
cards.back: Chembarambakkam, one of four reservoirs that fell to about 0.1% of capacity on Day Zero.

cards.front: What is this palm-leaf manuscript?
cards.back: The Arthashastra, attributed to Kautilya, rediscovered in 1905.

cards.front: Which Indian statistician is this, and what did his model prioritise?
cards.back: P. C. Mahalanobis: capital goods over consumer goods in the Second Five-Year Plan (1956).

cards.front: Which picture shows Bill Phillips with his machine, and which shows the MONIAC alone in a museum?
cards.back: First: Phillips at the LSE. Second: the MONIAC at the Science Museum.

cards.front: The phrase 'invisible hand' appears ___ in The Wealth of Nations.
cards.back: Only once.

cards.front: Herbert Simon (1971): a wealth of information creates a poverty of ___.
cards.back: Attention.

cards.front: Keynes (1930) predicted a working week of about ___ hours by 2030.
What did Gary Becker's 1965 time paper argue?
cards.back: Households combine goods and their own time; as wages rise, time gets dearer, so people buy time-saving goods.

cards.front: Minnesota Starvation Experiment: who, when, how many men?
cards.back: Ancel Keys, 1944 to 1945, 36 conscientious objectors cut to about 1,560 calories a day.

cards.front: What did the 2018 marshmallow test replication find?
cards.back: About half the original effect, mostly explained by family background.

cards.front: Kornai's term for why Soviet firms never economised?
cards.back: The soft budget constraint: losses would always be covered.

cards.front: NFSA 2013: how much grain per person per month, at what prices?
cards.back: 5 kg; rice ₹3, wheat ₹2, coarse grains ₹1 per kg (free since 2024 under PMGKAY to 2028).

cards.front: Why do kidney exchanges exist?
cards.back: Organ sales are banned, so price cannot allocate; swaps and chains match incompatible donor pairs. Alvin Roth, Nobel 2012.

cards.front: What is the Jevons paradox?
cards.back: Making use of a resource more efficient can increase total consumption of it. Jevons, The Coal Question, 1865.

cards.front: Who led India's Green Revolution and where did it start?
cards.back: M. S. Swaminathan with Borlaug's dwarf wheat; Punjab, 1966 to 1967.

cards.front: Who said guns will make us powerful, butter will only make us fat, and when?
cards.back: Hermann Göring, 1936. Goebbels said something similar that January.

cards.front: Why does the production frontier usually bow outward?
cards.back: Resources are not equally good at everything, so each extra unit of one good costs more and more of the other.

cards.front: China's share of rare earth refining and of permanent magnets (IEA 2024)?
cards.back: About 91% of refining, about 94% of sintered magnets.

cards.front: Why did memory chips get scarce in 2025 to 2026?
cards.back: AI servers bid for high-bandwidth memory, so makers shifted wafers away from ordinary DRAM.

cards.front: India's 2026-27 budget: spending and deficit target?
cards.back: About ₹53.5 lakh crore spending; fiscal deficit 4.3% of GDP.

cards.front: Origin of TANSTAAFL and its popularisers?
cards.back: Saloon free lunches; first printed 1933; Heinlein 1966; Friedman 1975.

cards.front: Marginal value theorem (Charnov, 1976): when should a forager leave a patch?
cards.back: When its rate of gain there falls to the average rate for the whole habitat.

cards.front: What does this bumblebee have to do with economics?
cards.back: Foraging animals face opportunity costs; Charnov's marginal value theorem predicts when to leave a patch.

quiz.prompt: Put these in order, earliest first.
You get a free, non-resellable Clapton ticket. Dylan plays the same night: ticket $40, worth $50 to you. Opportunity cost of seeing Clapton?
quiz.explanation: $10: Dylan's $50 value minus the $40 you would have paid.

quiz.prompt: What is this machine?
quiz.explanation: The MONIAC, or Phillips Machine, a hydraulic model of the economy from 1949.

quiz.prompt: This palm-leaf manuscript is a copy of which text?
quiz.explanation: The Arthashastra, rediscovered in 1905.

quiz.prompt: Who is this?
quiz.explanation: Elinor Ostrom, Nobel 2009, first woman economics laureate.

quiz.prompt: Which picture shows Thomas Malthus?
quiz.explanation: The second. The first is Adam Smith.

quiz.prompt: Match each economist to an idea.
quiz.explanation: Robbins 1932, Wieser 1914, Ricardo 1817, Sen 1981, Ostrom 1990.

quiz.prompt: Match each example to its allocation method.
quiz.explanation: Each method decides who bears scarcity differently.

quiz.prompt: India sent 20 tonnes of gold to Switzerland in 1991. Was the amount sent to the Bank of England higher or lower?
quiz.explanation: 47 tonnes went to the Bank of England.

quiz.prompt: Is China's share of world rare earth refining higher or lower than 75%?
quiz.explanation: About 91% (IEA, 2024).

quiz.prompt: Britain rationed bread during the Second World War.
quiz.explanation: Bread was rationed only after the war, 1946 to 1948.

quiz.prompt: In the Tamil Nadu study, the same farmers scored better on cognitive tests after harvest than before.
quiz.explanation: Before harvest, when money was tight, they scored worse.

quiz.prompt: Which of these was NOT a founder of the marginal revolution?
quiz.explanation: Adam Smith died in 1790; the marginalists wrote in the 1870s.

quiz.prompt: Which metal was NOT in the Simon-Ehrlich bet?
quiz.explanation: The five were copper, chromium, nickel, tin and tungsten.

quiz.prompt: Guess the person.
quiz.explanation: A. W. H. Phillips, builder of the MONIAC and author of the Phillips curve.
clues: Worked as a crocodile hunter in Australia.
Repaired a secret radio as a prisoner of war.
Built an economy out of water pipes.
A famous curve of unemployment and wages bears his name.

quiz.prompt: Guess the person.
quiz.explanation: Amartya Sen, Nobel 1998, Bharat Ratna 1999.
clues: Argued no famine has happened in a functioning democracy.

quiz.prompt: Drop a pin on the city that declared Day Zero in June 2019.
quiz.explanation: Chennai, Tamil Nadu.

quiz.prompt: Drop a pin on Bayan Obo, the world's largest rare earth mine.
quiz.explanation: Inner Mongolia, northern China.
